In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

CMV+ patients with NKG2C-expressing NK cells are at risk of developing de novo head/and neck or colorectal cancers, whereas patients with genitourinaty tumors are characterized by a standard NK signature.

the development of de novo specific tumors after OLT is linked to the modulation of NK cells, with an aberrant expansion and functional impairment of NKG2C+/IFN-γ−/TNF-α+ cells in patients diagnosed with head/neck and colorectal cancers and an immature NKG2A+/IFN-α+/TNF-α− phenotype associated with genitourinal tumors.
the development of de novo tumors post-OLT in the liver allograft is associated with the modulation of NK cell repertoire and function and the interplay with CMV status.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

NK cells from liver transplant recipients are characterized by a unique phenotype, which is associated with a distinct cytokine production pattern, and that these features may impact on the development of specific malignancies.
NK cells are not just a bystander in the development of de novo malignancies after OLT.
NK cells are not only involved in the surveillance of viral infections and tumor development, but also in the control of tumor growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the development of a specific de novo cancer after OLT may be linked to a particular modulation of NK cell subsets.
NK cells are not only involved in the control of viral infections, but also play a key role in the immune control of specific tumors.
NK cells may play a key role in the development of specific malignancies after OLT.
